segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning the things you wrote about:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But because of the cases of sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman should have her own husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The husband should give his wife what is owed her, and likewise the wife her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wife does not have authority over her own body; her husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body; his wife does.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer and then be together again, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this as a concession, not as a command.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wish that everyone were as I myself am. But each person has their own gift from God, one of this kind and another of that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the unmarried and the widows I say: it is good for them if they remain as I am.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if they are not exercising self-control, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the married I give this instruction—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but if she does separate, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband should not divorce his wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the rest I say—I, not the Lord—if any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the unbelieving husband has been made holy through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been made holy through the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if the unbeliever separates, let him separate. The brother or the sister is not enslaved in such cases; God has called us to peace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only, as the Lord has apportioned to each, as God has called each, so let each one walk. And this is what I direct in all the assemblies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Was anyone called when already circumcised? He should not undo his circumcision. Has anyone been called while uncircumcised? He should not be circumcised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing; what counts is keeping God’s commandments.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Each person should remain in the calling in which they were called.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you. But if you are in fact able to become free, rather take the opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freed person; likewise the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, in whatever condition each was called, in that let each remain with God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now concerning the virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is faithful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I think, then, that this is good because of the present distress: that it is good for a person to stay as they are.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if the virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh, and I am trying to spare you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean, brothers and sisters, is this: the time has been cut short. From now on, even those who have wives should be as though they had none,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they did not own,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and those who make use of the world as though they were not making full use of it. For the form of this world is passing away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I want you to be free of concern. The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he is divided. The unmarried woman, and the virgin, is concerned with the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and in spirit; but the married woman is concerned with the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I say this for your own benefit, not to throw a noose around you, but for the sake of what is proper and of undistracted devotion to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is passing her prime and so it ought to be, let him do what he wishes; he is not sinning. Let them marry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who stands firm in his heart, under no compulsion but having authority over his own will, and has decided this in his own heart, to keep his virgin as she is, will do well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, the one who marries his virgin does well, and the one who does not marry will do better.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A wife is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is free to be married to whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she is more blessed if she remains as she is, in my judgment; and I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

notes.phrase: It is good for a man not to touch a woman
notes.traditional: It is good for a man not to touch a woman (read as Paul's own statement)
notes.note: The Greek has no quotation marks, and older translations read this as Paul's own view. Most recent scholars take it as a line from the Corinthians' letter that Paul quotes and then qualifies in verses 2–5, and the text is punctuated that way here; the other reading remains possible. 'Touch a woman' was an established euphemism for sexual intercourse, not for marriage or for physical contact in general.

notes.traditional: to burn (KJV); to burn with passion (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek says only 'to burn'. Most interpreters understand burning with sexual desire, and many translations add 'with passion'. A minority take it as burning in judgment, so the bare verb is kept.

Greek and Roman law had no category of separation short of divorce: a spouse who left the marriage had ended it, and 'separate' was an ordinary word for divorcing. 'Not I, but the Lord' points to Jesus' own teaching against divorce, preserved in the Gospels (for example Mark 10:2–12). In verse 12 Paul marks where he goes beyond what that teaching addressed.

The verb is from the same root as the 'holy' said of the children at the end of the verse, and 'made holy' keeps that link visible where 'sanctified' hides it. Paul does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved, since verse 16 treats that as still open. The usual view is that the marriage and its children fall within the sphere of God's people rather than defiling the believer, though exactly what Paul means is debated.

notes.traditional: called us (KJV, NASB); called you (ESV, NIV, NRSV)
notes.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'us' and 'you', which differ by one letter in Greek and were pronounced alike. SBLGNT reads 'us'; several other critical editions and many modern translations read 'you'. The sense is hardly affected.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word appears as one English word.

notes.traditional: become uncircumcised; remove the marks of circumcision
notes.note: The verb refers to a known procedure for stretching or restoring the foreskin. Some Jewish men underwent it to avoid ridicule in the Greek gymnasium and baths, where men exercised and bathed naked. 1 Maccabees 1:15 mentions the practice.

notes.traditional: use it rather (KJV); avail yourself of the opportunity
notes.note: The Greek says only 'rather make use', with no object. Most modern translators and commentators supply 'the chance of freedom', as here. A substantial minority, ancient and modern, supply 'your slavery': 'even if you can become free, make use of your present condition instead'. The grammar permits both; the tense of the verb and the 'but' that opens the clause are usually thought to favour the first.

The participle can mean 'present' or 'impending', and the noun covers necessity, hardship and crisis. Some think Paul means a local hardship at Corinth, such as a food shortage. Others think he means the pressures of the last days, which verses 29–31 have in view. The rendering leaves this open.

notes.traditional: There is difference also between a wife and a virgin (KJV)
notes.note: The manuscripts vary considerably in wording and punctuation at this point. The text followed here attaches 'and he is divided' to the married man of verse 33 and begins a new sentence about the unmarried woman and the virgin. The reading behind the KJV instead makes 'divided' the start of a statement that wife and virgin differ. Most modern editions and translations agree with the reading adopted here.

notes.traditional: his virgin (KJV); his virgin daughter (NASB); his betrothed (ESV), his fiancée (NRSV)
notes.note: Verses 36–38 are among the most disputed in Paul. The older view is that a father is deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage, and the verb in verse 38 normally means 'give in marriage'. Most recent scholars think an engaged man is deciding whether to marry his fiancée, which suits 'let them marry' here, and they argue that the verb in verse 38 could by this period also mean simply 'marry'. The translation follows the second view but keeps Paul's own word 'virgin', as in verse 25.

notes.phrase: if she is passing her prime
notes.traditional: if she pass the flower of her age (KJV); if his passions are strong (ESV, NRSV)
notes.note: The adjective is rare. Its attested uses and related words refer to being past the bloom of youth, which for a woman meant past the usual age for marriage; that sense is followed here. Many modern translations instead take the man as the subject and render 'if his passions are strong', which is also possible and fits the stress on self-mastery in verse 37.

The Greek verb is literally 'fall asleep', a common euphemism for dying which Paul uses repeatedly of believers (for example in chapter 15). Most translations render it 'dies' here. The image is kept so that the same expression reads the same way throughout the letter.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation, and translators vary between 'fornication', 'sexual immorality', 'prostitution' and 'unchastity', which obscures that one Greek word lies behind them.
Traditional 'servant' or 'bondservant' softens a word that meant a slave in the first century, and it recurs in parables, in Paul's self-descriptions and in household instructions.

The plural address to mixed communities and the singular for a fellow believer occur throughout the letters, and the choice between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers' should be made once.
The sleep euphemism for death recurs in the Gospels, Acts, 1 Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians, and translations alternate between 'die' and 'fall asleep', sometimes within one book.
The word ranges from the physical body and ordinary human life to Paul's term for humanity opposed to God, and translations vary widely ('flesh', 'sinful nature', 'this life', 'body').
